draft.title: Population density
card: Population density is the number of people living in each square kilometre of an area. Density = population ÷ area in square kilometres.
A place with many people in a small area has a high density. A place with few people in a large area has a low density.
A map can shade each area by its density. Darker shading usually shows a higher density, and a legend explains each shade.
Density is an average for the whole area. It does not show where people live inside that area.
draft.remember: Density is people divided by area, and shading on a map shows where it is high or low.

a.q: Town A has 5000 people in 10 square kilometres. Town B has 5000 people in 50 square kilometres. How do their densities compare?
opts: Town A is higher, as its people share a smaller area
Town B is higher, as its people have a larger area
They are equal, as both towns have 5000 people
Town B is higher, as it has more room for people
a.why: Town A has 500 people per square kilometre and Town B has 100. The same population in a smaller area gives a higher density. Equal populations do not mean equal densities, because area matters too.
a.clue: Divide each population by its area.

b.q: A map of Western Australia shades the Perth region dark and the Kimberley region very pale. What does this show?
opts: More people per square kilometre live around Perth
The Kimberley has a larger total population than Perth
The Kimberley has more people per square kilometre
Everyone in the Perth region lives in the same spot
b.why: Dark shading usually means a higher density, so Perth has more people per square kilometre. Pale shading shows few people per square kilometre, not a larger total. Density is an average, so the map cannot show exactly where people live inside the Perth region.
b.clue: Check what darker shading usually shows on a density map.

a.best: Town A is higher, as its people share a smaller area

b.best: More people per square kilometre live around Perth
